→ ConnectWise warns attacks on ScreenConnect continue against unpatched systems
→ CVE-2026-84869, a critical client flaw (CVSS 9.9), is fixed in version 26.6.5
→ ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions (Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+ and two Password Link add-ons) across 400 partner environments; having them doesn't by itself mean compromise
→ Huntress saw a spike in SCKit toolkit activity on 13 Nov: 205 hosts across 41 organisations
→ ConnectWise: disabling extensions and updating "do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established"

My take: patching the server isn't the end here. I'd treat every partner instance with those extensions as possibly compromised and hunt for rogue services, because updates don't remove access already gained.

What to do: update to 26.6.5 or later, disable the listed extensions and don't re-enable them, then look for unexpected services and remote clients on endpoints.

items.take: Most AI gateways I'd audit first for one thing: the default admin key. Teams treat LiteLLM or Dify as a dev toy, but they hold every provider key you own. Treat them as production.

cover.hook: AI agents are hunting your AI apps. For the API keys.
cover.sub: Amazon's decoy servers, posing as LLM services, logged AI agents probing LiteLLM, Dify, Ollama and more.

slides.title: The decoys
slides.body: Amazon threat intelligence ran decoy servers (its MadPot network) posing as popular LLM services. They logged requests from 3 October to late last week. Amazon has moderate confidence the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI pentesting tool.

slides.title: The targets
slides.body: One API, New API, LiteLLM, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, Ollama and more. The playbook: default admin credentials, unfinished installs, known flaws such as Langflow CVE-2025-3248, secrets in env files and client-side JS.

slides.label: new techniques
slides.note: Amazon: "None of the techniques in these campaigns were new." What changes is speed and persistence.

slides.title: Not just decoys
slides.body: Cloudflare saw an ARTEX-driven attacker use a stolen CI/CD API token with no IP limits: 400 database dump requests in an hour. Amazon says it cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported in its decoy logs.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Change default admin keys (LiteLLM master key)
Add expiry + IP limits to API tokens

items.ig_caption:
A DNS security company. Breached through its data migration vendor. 📦

What Security Affairs reported (17 Nov):
→ Infoblox confirmed unauthorized access to certain company information through "a compromised third-party data migration vendor"
→ The Register, citing sources, says the vendor had SharePoint migration access and its accounts were used to take data
→ Reported data: NIOS configuration snapshots (DNS and DHCP configs) for some customers, plus staff Social Security numbers and bank details
→ Infoblox says it has no indication its products, cloud services, software updates or build process were involved
→ It hasn't named the vendor or said how many people are affected

My take: migration vendors get broad, temporary access that nobody remembers to take back. I'd list every vendor account in Microsoft 365 today and remove any whose project is finished.

What to do: if you're an Infoblox customer, watch for their notice and review what your exported configs contain. Everyone: put end dates on vendor accounts.
